interject

/in-ter-JEKT/ - the stress falls on JEKT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Interject means to insert a remark into a conversation.

Court reporters dread twins on the witness stand: each will interject a correction the instant the other rounds a number up.

Worked Example

The documentary crew learned to leave gaps in the narration, because the lighthouse keeper would interject a detail at every pause — the year of the wreck, the name of the dog that swam ashore — quick footnotes dropped into the story without ever stopping it.

To interject is to slip a remark into talk that is already moving — a quick aside, correction or joke tucked into a pause. It is gentler than interrupt: the interrupter takes the floor away, while the interjector adds something and lets the speaker roll on.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

interpose: To interpose is to place a remark — or yourself — between other speakers, stepping briefly into their exchange. It is stiffer and more formal than interject, at home in committee minutes and diplomatic notes, and it still defers to the speakers around it, as an interjection does.

blurt: To blurt is to let a remark burst out unplanned — the words escape before judgment catches them. To interject can be perfectly deliberate: the speaker waits for the right pause and places the remark exactly there. Blurting is an accident of timing; interjecting is timing used well.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

refrain: to hold your remark back on purpose

listen: to take the talk in rather than add to it

Where it sits · how much it disturbs the speaker's turn — comment → interject → interrupt

comment vs. interject: A comment waits its turn and enters when the floor is free; it stops short of interject, which slides a remark into a live pause.

interrupt vs. interject: Interrupt goes further than a comment ever does — it cuts the speaker off mid-sentence and takes the floor, precisely the shove an interjection avoids.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — inter

Prefix — inter: between (Latin)

Root — ject

Root — ject: to throw (Latin jacere)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin inter- ('between') plus jacere ('to throw') makes interject: to throw a remark between the pieces of someone else's sentence. The same ject- does heavy lifting all over English — eject throws out, reject throws back — and here the thing thrown is a word, aimed at a gap in the conversation.

Use the root in a new word: eject

Use the root in a new word: eject: The umpire ejected the arguing manager before the fifth inning was over.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Interject is the polite technician's word for slipping a remark into moving conversation. If the speaker gets cut off, say interrupt; if the remark escapes without planning, blurt. Meetings, interviews and transcripts love interject because it describes the move without blaming anyone.
